format: html

## Overview

This document summarizes the methods and findings for Task 4. We developed two text-classification models—a binary classifier and a multi-class classifier—using Support Vector Machines (SVMs). The goal was to identify whether HTML pages contain relevant claim content and, if so, to predict the appropriate claim category.

## Text Preprocessing
In SVM:
We applied a standardized preprocessing pipeline to all documents. First, we parsed HTML files to extract text from paragraph and header tags. We then cleaned the text by removing URLs, punctuation, digits, and extra whitespace, followed by lowercasing. The cleaned text was tokenized, stopwords were removed, and tokens were lemmatized. From the training data, we selected the top 1000 most frequent terms and computed TF-IDF features. Finally, we applied z-score scaling to all features using training-set statistics.

## Predictive Models

We trained two linear-kernel SVM models using the 1000 TF-IDF features:

- **Binary Classification Model**: Predicts whether a document contains relevant claim content.
- **Multi-class Classification Model**: Assigns documents to one of several claim categories.

Both models used standard linear SVMs without additional hyperparameter tuning.

## Model Performance

Using an 80/20 train-validation split, we estimated predictive accuracy for each model:

| Model | Estimated Accuracy |
|-------|-------------------|
| Binary Classification | 69.7% |
| Multi-class Classification | 68.0% |

## Key Findings

1. The binary SVM achieved roughly 70% accuracy, outperforming earlier baseline approaches from Task 1.
2. The multi-class SVM reached 68% accuracy, showing reasonable performance given the more challenging prediction task.
3. TF-IDF features combined with z-score scaling provided effective representations, allowing simple linear SVMs to perform well without extensive tuning.
